analysis.one_liner: Voids Labor Department rules that ease proof requirements for coal miners' black lung benefit claims.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with no cosponsors, it died in a House subcommittee at the end of the 102nd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Coal miners disabled by black lung disease can win benefits more easily under Labor Department rules that create presumptions: if a miner worked enough years in the mines, the law presumes the disease came from mining unless the employer proves otherwise. H.R. 3003 would have wiped out two of those presumption rules and barred the Labor Secretary from issuing any similar rule, making it harder for sick miners and their families to qualify for benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mine operators and employers who pay black lung benefits through premiums and excise taxes, because with the presumption rules voided, more sick miners would fail to prove their claims and fewer benefit payments would be owed.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that the two Labor Department regulations governing how claim adjudication presumptions work (20 C.F.R. 727.203(b)(3) and (b)(4)) have no force or effect. [S2] [S3]
It also bars the Secretary of Labor from promulgating any future regulation with the same legal effect, so the stricter proof standard could not simply be restored by rulemaking. [S3]

The bill's stated premise is that these regulations are not in accordance with section 402(f)(2) of the Black Lung Benefits Act — that is, that the Department read the statute more broadly than Congress wrote it, shifting the evidentiary burden in miners' favor. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Coal miners disabled by pneumoconiosis and their surviving families, who would face a harder path to proving their claims and could lose or never receive benefits, since the rules being voided are the ones that presume a long-tenured miner's disease arose from coal mine employment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Disabled coal miners and their families

drawbacks.text: By removing the presumption rules, the bill would force many long-tenured miners to prove the precise cause of a disease whose medical origin is often difficult to establish decades after exposure, making benefit denials more likely. [S2] [S3]

The strongest good-faith case for the bill — that the regulations exceed the statutory text of section 402(f)(2) — is itself the honest cost: the bill does not fix the underlying rules dispute in both directions, it simply zeroes out the regulations and locks the stricter reading in place. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit goes to the employers who fund black lung benefit payments, while its cost falls on sick miners and widows seeking compensation for an occupational disease. The bill presents this as correcting regulations that overreach the statute, but it offers no substitute standard for miners, so the practical effect is to make qualifying for benefits harder. Because it never advanced, no such change took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and died there when the 102nd Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert E. Wise Jr. of West Virginia introduced the bill on July 23, 1991. [S1] [S3]
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor. [S1] [S5]
On August 13, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, where it stayed with no further action. [S5]
No cosponsors signed on, no committee markup or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993. [S4] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Labor Department's presumption rules stayed in effect, so black lung claimants kept the easier path to benefits they had been using. Coal operators did not get the narrower proof standard they would have gained from the bill.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Wise Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to void the Labor Department's black lung adjudication regulations.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one besides the sponsor took a position on the record, so the partisan shape of the fight never formed.

industries.note: Operators fund black lung benefit payments, and voiding the presumption rules would have lowered how many sick miners qualify and how much they must pay. The bill's failure means that cost relief never arrived.

industries.industry: Coal miners with black lung disease and their families
industries.note: The bill would have taken away the rules that presume a long-tenured miner's disease came from coal mining, making claims harder to win. Its death preserved their existing path to benefits.
